en: Vārāha Gṛhyasūtra, 1: Hereafter follow the supplements to the Maitrāyaṇīya Sūtra: the person for domestic rites and expiation.

The twenty-two titles of the *pariśiṣṭas* (supplements) are: Anugrahika, Hautṛka, Śaulbika, Uttareṣṭaka, Vaiṣṇava, Ādhvaryavika, Cāturhotṛka, Gonāmika, Kulapāda, Rahasyapratigraha, Yamaka, Vṛṣotsarga, Praśna, Draviṇa, Ṣaṭkāraṇa, Pradhāna, Sāṃdehika, Pravara-adhyāya, Rudravidhāna, Chando’nukramaṇī, Antaryakalpa, Pravāsavidhi, Prātarupasthāna, and Bhūtotpatti.
One should perform the *pākayajñas* in the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*).
Because of its brevity, it is a *pākayajña*;
for they call what is brief "cooked" (*pāka*).
The rule for the *pākayajña* has the new- and full-moon sacrifices as its archetype; it is without *prayāja*s, without *anuyāja*s, and without *sāmidhenī* verses.

The oblations are performed after pronouncing [the mantra] ending with *svāhā*. (VGrs 1.5) One who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should perform them in the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*); one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) should do so in the hall fire (*śālāgni*). (VGrs 1.6) Having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, he should make a mark on it the size of an arrow. With the words "In the seat of truth," he draws a line from the rear half toward the north.
With the words "Seated in the Truth," he places one [brick] from the southern half facing east; with the words "Seated in the Heat," one from the northern half facing east;
and in the middle, two or three facing east.
With "Full of vigor," [he takes] the southern one; with "Full of milk," the northern one;
or [he takes] from the middle with "For Indra, thee."
He should scrape [the ground] with a blade of *darbha* grass, making all [lines] one span long.
Having sprinkled it with water, he places the fire upon it.

Having swept around it, strewn [grass] around it, and sprinkled water around it, he silently binds the fuel and sacrificial grass together; then he spreads them out with an odd number of bundles, with their tips pointing eastward, beginning from the south, and arranged from south to north.

Having seated the Brahman priest to the south of the fire and a vessel of water to the north, he prepares two strainers from *barhis* grass. With the formula, "You two are strainers belonging to Viṣṇu," he takes two blades of *darbha* grass that are equal in length, with unbroken ends, and measuring a span, using a plant for [the cutting].

Having cut [the grass] with the formula "By Viṣṇu's mind you are purified," and having wiped [the vessels] three times with water, he consecrates the *prokṣaṇī* waters according to the ritual rules (*dharmas*), brings forward the *praṇītā* water, and performs the pouring out, sprinkling, and mixing [of the grains]. Having placed the *caru* on the fire for each respective deity, he wipes the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, sprinkles them, heats them over the fire, and places the clarified butter (*ājya*) on the fire with the formula: "Aditi art thou, whose wings are unbroken. (VGrs 1.12)

With the formula, "Thou art the milk of Pṛśni," he pours out the clarified butter (ājya). With the verse, "The lord of booty... and so forth, he carries fire three times around both the clarified butter and the sacrificial oblation (havis).
With the formula, "May the god Savitṛ purify thee," he cooks the clarified butter.
Having silently sprinkled the fuel and the sacrificial grass, he spreads them around as prescribed.
He places the enclosing sticks around [the fire].
Having looked at the clarified butter with the words, "Thou art splendor," he sets it down on the darbha grass behind the fire.
Having sprinkled [the clarified butter] over it, he sets down the *sthālīpāka* to the north.
Having placed the fuel-stick once only, the *vairūpākṣa* formula is the first of the oblations.

Having addressed the *brahmán*, having placed the fuel-stick, having poured the two libations (*āghāra*), having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), and having joined [the fire] with the verse "I yoke thee," [he proceeds].
For it is known that one who is not yoked does not carry the oblation.
At will, he offers before the pole with [the verse]:
"Yoked, O Jātavedas, carry [the offering] from the front; know this which is being performed here."
"You are the physician of the medicine; you are its protector. Inspired by you, may we win cattle, horses, and men.
Svāhā! Thus.
"O Agni, through you may we cross over all enmity, as one crosses over streams of water. (VGrs 1.24)
Having sacrificed to the lunar mansion, one should sacrifice to the deity,
the day-and-night, the season, and the lunar day.
Having sprinkled clarified butter over the oblation, whatever its deity may be, one should offer it to that deity, along with the *caru* offering according to the respective deity.
"To Ākūti, svāhā!
To Ākūti, svāhā!"—with these words he should offer the Jaya oblations.
Prajāpati bestowed them.

With the verse "iḍām agne," he should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation in the eastern part of the northern half [of the fire]. He should place the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*), the supporting-vessel (*upayāma*), and the two strainers (*pavitra*) together [on the altar]. [He recites: "May Anumati favor us today... VGrs_1.28–29. "O Anumati, follow after us," [he says];
and he offers the expiatory oblations with "Bhūḥ svāhā! and "Thou, O Agni... [and so forth].
So may you, O Agni, [grant] us [this]: "The mind is light;
there are thirty-three threads."
And with the mantra, "O Agni, you are the unaging one...
(VS 1.31): "Suck this honeyed breast, swelling with water, O Agni, in the midst of the flood;
enjoy the honeyed spring, the wave, and enter your oceanic dwelling."
"svāhā!"—
with these words he makes an offering over the release of the enclosing sticks.
"O Lord of Food," with these words he should offer a portion of food.

He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the mantra: "Thou art fuel; may we prosper, svāhā! He places a second stick with the mantra: "Thou art a kindler; may we be kindled. He should pour out the full vessel upon the sacrificial grass.
This is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
This is the ritual procedure for the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña).
Having performed the purification with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha," he should sprinkle water around the fire.
The bride-price is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should know that the bride-price is a horse; some say it is a cow. (VGrs 1.39)

Having prepared the lying-in chamber facing either east or north, he should cause her to enter it at the [proper] time with the words: "I resort to the Firm; I resort to the Auspicious; I resort to Hope. With the two verses beginning "The seed and the urine," he should touch her right side with the words: "I resort to the Firm; I resort to the Auspicious; I resort to Hope.
He should touch her right side with the two verses beginning "The seed and the urine."
Or he may cause [the Veda] to be heard.

When a son has been born, once he has bathed immediately thereafter, the mother shall not touch him until the application of the mantras. To the west of the fire that has been kindled, swept around, and strewn with grass, [he places] the boy on a new, unwashed garment with his head facing east.
Having laid him down on his back and having folded a middle leaf of a *palāśa* tree, he should whisper into his ears with it: "Bhūḥ! I place [it] in you," into the right ear;
"Bhuvaḥ! I place [it] in you," into the left ear.
"May I place *svaḥ* in you," [he says] over the right [hand];
"bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, may I place [them] in you," [he says] over the left. Then they both address him with these mantras.
Become a stone, become an axe, become invincible gold.
From limb after limb you arise; from the heart you are born.
You are indeed the self named "son"; live for a hundred autumns.
Thus [it is said].
Wherever he lies, let him touch that place with: "O Earth, I know your heart; it rests in the moon in heaven.
The gods know the nectar of immortality; may I not weep for the loss of a son."
Thus:

Having prepared the clarified butter (ājya), having addressed the Brahman priest, having placed a fuel-stick (samidh) on the fire, having poured the two libations (āghāra), and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he should offer four oblations of clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis.
Some [teachers] say that he should also offer the Jaya, Abhyātāna, and Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations.
Having poured the remnants of the oblations into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, and having rubbed gold against it, he should make the boy eat from it four times while reciting the Vyāhṛtis.
According to some, the eating of gold should be done by rubbing it in water until the end of the twelfth year.
"Make the nourishment swell."
Saying "May you swell with strength," he should wash his two breasts and suckle [the child],
first the right one and then the left.
Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and the expiation oblations, and having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he sprinkles water around it.
This is the ritual procedure at the outer gate: a perpetual fire is maintained there;
one should offer oblations of *kaṇa*, mustard seeds, and barley with the *vyāhṛtis*.
One should mutter the *Apratiratha* hymn and the six-verse hymn beginning with "Indro bhūtasya.
At the appropriate time, one should sprinkle water all around the lying-in chamber.

Vārāhagṛhyasūtra, 3: Having performed [the rites] in this very same way on the tenth day, the father and mother should give a name to the son— one beginning with a voiced consonant, having a semi-vowel in the middle, ending in a long vowel or a nasal (abhiniṣṭāna), being a *kṛt*-derived form and not a *taddhita* derivative, consisting of either two or four syllables, and excluding [names] belonging to the father.
The names [of the children] should be derived from the name of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or the deity; or they may have two names. A Brāhmaṇa, however, should have two names.

The name of a girl should consist of a single word, with the vowel *a* inserted between syllables, ending in long *ā*, having an odd number of syllables, and excluding those named after rivers, lunar mansions, the moon, the sun, Pūṣan, Devadatta, or Rakṣita.
Having smeared his hands with fresh butter, he should touch him [the boy] while reciting: "With the splendor of Soma, I touch thee.
(VGrs 3.4) In all rites for a boy, there is a cooked offering (*sthālīpāka*) dedicated either to Agni or to Prajāpati.
(VGrs 3.5) In all cases where no deity is specified, the deity is Agni for males and Aryaman for females. (VGrs 3.6)
For one year, the mother and father shall not eat meat.
(VGrs 3.7) When a son’s teeth have emerged, one should sacrifice to Agni with a cow or a domestic animal.
(VGrs 3.8) Having returned from a journey abroad, one should smell the head of one's son three times, saying: "I smell you with the *hiṃkāra* of cattle. (VGrs 3.9)
As at the birth-rite, having inserted his finger [into the child's ear], he should whisper [the mantra] into his ears.
Then he consecrates him with the mantra, "Become a stone.
Having sacrificed with a goat and a ram to Agni and Dhanvantari while observing the vow for a son, he should have the boy eat [of the sacrificial food] four times with the long Vyāhṛtis.
And [he recites] "O giver of life... (Āyurdā deva).
The rites for a boy (*kumāra-karman*) are performed during the bright fortnight, during the northern course of the sun, under an auspicious lunar mansion, avoiding the ninth day.
All seasons are suitable for marriage, except for the months of Māgha and Caitra, and the latter part of the summer.
Having caused [the boy] to touch [the fire], they offer the oblation.
In the third year, they fashion matted locks.
Or as in the *Kulakalpa*:

Having established the fire, swept around it, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, he seats the *brahmán* to the south of the fire and a vessel of water containing *śamī* and *śamaka* to the north. Then he addresses him with the four verses beginning, "Golden-hued, pure... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ*).
With the section beginning "The plants which... and the verse: "May the divine waters be for our aid; may they be auspicious for our drinking;
may they flow toward us with health and well-being."
May the dear waters of the desert be auspicious to us; may the waters of the rivers be auspicious to us.
May the waters of the ocean be auspicious to us, and may the waters of the wells be auspicious to us.
May Mitra be auspicious to us, may Varuṇa be auspicious to us, and may Aryaman be auspicious to us.
"May Indra and Agni be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us.
With these words, one should perform for them the rites involving water: sprinkling around, pouring over, and bathing.

Having consecrated the clarified butter, having addressed the Brahman priest, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, having poured the two libations (āghāra), and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he offers seven oblations with the seven verses beginning "Agni purifies the lives" (agnā āyūṃṣi pavase), and also with the verse "O giver of life" (āyurdā deva). [He recites:
"Those long-haired ones who first sat for the sacrificial session, by whom this world is encompassed and shines forth..."
"I offer these to them for long life, for longevity, and for well-being"—
thus [he says], and also with the *vyāhṛtis*.
The ritual action has been explained by what preceded.
[He should say: "O wind, provide with cold water;

O wind, provide with warm water. Having mixed the heated [water] with the others, he should consecrate the waters while reciting: "You are givers of moisture, givers of life; grant us prosperity and food. Then he should moisten the hair-parting on the right side.
"May Aditi shave the hair; may the waters moisten it for life, for long life, and for well-being. (VGrs 4.8)
He places a blade of darbha grass with its tip pointing upward at the right side of the hair-parting.
He inserts a blade of darbha grass between [the head and the razor], saying, "O herb, protect him!
He applies the razor, saying, "O razor, do not harm him!"
With that razor with which the wise Savitṛ shaved King Soma and Varuṇa,
with that, O Brahmans, shave this [hair] of his, so that he may be long-lived and reach old age—
[I am so-and-so].
Thus he shaves. To the south, the mother or another non-widowed woman should gather the hair that has not reached the ground with bull’s dung.
"May this luster not follow after your hair; may Dhātṛ establish it for you thus."
"May Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ bestow splendor upon you. With this, he consecrates the water as it flows away.
By that same rite, having again consecrated the water, he should pour it over another part of the hair-line and then over the upper part.
But the other two [formulas] for shaving are those with which Pūṣan shaved for the sake of the longevity of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra:
"With that I shave you for long life, for longevity, and for well-being"—
thus [he says] behind.
"With that by which he moves further and beholds the sun for a long time,
with that I besmear you for the sake of life, for long-livedness, for good renown, and for great splendor.
Thus [he besmears] from the north.
"With the well-fashioned razor that shaves, O barber, as you shave the hair, cleanse the head; do not steal away his life-force.
With these words, he hands over the iron razor to the hair-cutter.

They arrange their hair according to their respective lineages: the Vasiṣṭhas wear their hair in a single braid on the right; the Atris, Bhṛgus, and Kaśyapas wear it braided on both sides; the Āṅgirasas have five tufts; and others wear a single topknot.
Some keep a horse for the sake of auspiciousness. [The mantra:
"The triple life-span of Kaśyapa, the triple life-span of Jamadagni, the triple life-span of Agastya."
"May that which is the threefold life-span of the gods be mine for a hundred years"—
with these words he touches his head.
Having gathered cow-dung, he should place it in a corner of the house toward the northeast, between the house and a stack of straw.
Or at a non-empty shaving:
having shaved the hair-ends, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and Indra found for King Varuṇa a great place of rest between heaven and earth, within the waters, in the sky. VGrs 4.21
Thus,
he gives a boon to the officiant.
He gives a tuft of eyelashes and sesame paste for the shaving of the hair.
For one year, the mother shall not eat sour food;
she shall not eat out of anger;
and she shall remain silent, except for salt.
For a maiden, [the rite is performed] excluding the oblation.
(VGrs 4.25) He should cause learned Brāhmaṇas to pronounce words for the accomplishment of his purpose.
(VGrs 4.26) The same applies to the subsequent [rites]. (VGrs 4.27)
In the *Vārāhagṛhyasūtra*, 5.1:
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
or in the sixth, the seventh, or the fifth.

Then, one should initiate a Kṣatriya in the eleventh year from conception and a Vaiśya in the twelfth year from conception. Before the sixteenth year for a Brāhmaṇa, before the twenty-second for a Kṣatriya, and before the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya, the Sāvitrī has not been lost; beyond these ages, they become fallen from the Sāvitrī.
One should not perform sacrifices for them, nor teach them, nor carry their corpses out, nor give their daughters in marriage.
(VGrs 5.3) The making of the matted locks is internal; the initiation (*upanayana*) is external. (VGrs 5.4) The consecration by fire and that of the *brahman* have been explained. (VGrs 5.5)

Having shaved the boy's hair and bathed him, with his head anointed, and having had him sip water according to the ritual rules for sipping, he should place him to the south of the fire and, while reciting "I have performed [the praise] of Dadhikrāvan," make the boy eat curd three times. Then [he recites]:
"Driving away ill-spoken words, purifying our pure color, she has come to us."
Bestowing strength through the out-breath and the in-breath, this auspicious, fortunate goddess is my girdle.

Guardian of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), overcomer of ascetic fervor (*tapas*), she slays the demon and overcomes the enemies. As such, O auspicious one, go around me on all sides; O fortunate girdle, may we, who uphold you, suffer no harm.
Thus he ties on the girdle: a triple-stranded one made of muñja grass, wound three times around, for the [initiate];
a bowstring made of mūrvā for a Kṣatriya; and one made of hemp for a Vaiśya.
"Thou art the sacrificial thread; with thee, the sacrificial thread, I invest thee"—with these words, he puts on the *yajñopavīta*.
Those goddesses who spun, who stretched, who wove, who brought forth, and those goddesses who spun the borders all around the fire—may those goddesses clothe you for old age.
Long-lived, put on this garment; put on splendor.
"Make him one who lives a hundred years, grant him long life;
live for a hundred abundant autumns, and as one worthy of wealth, may you distribute riches and prosper.
Having thus clothed him in a new garment, [he recites: "The eye of Mitra, the upholder, more powerful, glorious, steadfast, and bold."
"I have put on this garment, which is unwashed, moving, and fit for a prize-winner; it is a prize-winner itself. Thus [he puts on] the black antelope skin.

Having prepared the clarified butter, having addressed the Brahman priest, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, having poured the two libations (āghāra), and having offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he should offer eight oblations pertaining to the tonsure of the matted locks.
And with the *vyāhṛtis*.
The conclusion of the ritual action has been stated previously.
[He should say: "For Time, for you; for the lineage, for you; for victory, for you; for emergence, for you; for the eating of food, for you—thus he should wash [the hands]."
Having filled his joined palms with water and washed his hands with the words, "For the sake of good action," he sips water with the words, "Here I cause Duryaman to sink," and then spits it out.
With the words, "May I be superior to my rivals and my enemies," he does so a second time.
"In the morning we shall invoke the fierce Bhaga, the victorious son of Aditi, the distributor; may even the weak man, the one who thinks himself swift, and even the king enjoy Bhaga"—thus he says;
with these words, one should worship the Āditya.
"I have entered the life of sacred study (*brahmacarya*); please call upon me," he should say.
[The teacher replies: "Come, O Brahman; approach the Brahman. I, being a Brahman, initiate you who are a Brahman, [Name]!
Then he takes his name, which is to be used for formal salutation.

"In the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand, O [Name]!"—with these words, he should take his right hand with his own right hand, palm upwards, grasping the thumb and the hair-side of the fingers.
"May your mind follow me alone; may you indeed follow me."

"May your heart, which is [fixed] upon me, blaze like [ghee] poured into the fire"—looking at him as he gazes thus, she should place her hand behind his back, take hold of the region of his heart, and mutter: "You are the knot of the vital breaths; may you not loosen."

With the words, "Thou art the knot of Brahmā," [he touches] the region of the navel. "We invoke thee, the Lord of hosts, the sage among sages, possessed of most exalted fame, the supreme ruler, the priest, O Brahmaṇaspati; making us [prosperous] with thy aids, sit upon thy seat."
Thus he should circumambulate the fire, keeping it to his right.
He sits down on *darbha* grass to the west of the fire, and the religious student (*brahmacārī*) sits to the south.
Having sat down, he mutters, "Teach me, sir! (VGrs 5.24).
Having bent his right knee, joined his hands with *darbha* grass in them, and uttered "Oṃ," he should recite the *vyāhṛtis* and the *Sāvitrī*.
This is likewise the case for the recitation of the *kāṇḍas*.
For a Brāhmaṇa, he should recite the *Gāyatrī*: "Tat savitur vareṇyam."

For a Kṣatriya, [he recites] the Triṣṭubh verse beginning with "May the god Savitṛ come, rich in jewels"; for a Vaiśya, the Jagatī verse beginning with "They harness the mind. He recites [the verses] by quarters, then by half-verses, and finally the whole verse at the end.
He gives a staff of *pālāśa* wood to a Brāhmaṇa, one of *naiyagrodha* wood to a Kṣatriya, and one of *aśvattha* wood to a Vaiśya. [The formula is:
"O you of good fame, make me of good fame!
As you, O you of good fame, are of good fame, so may I become of good fame."
"Just as you are the guardian of the treasure of the Veda for the gods, so may I be the guardian of the treasure of Brahman for human beings"—with these words he accepts it.
The water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) of a Brāhmaṇa has its opening facing upward; that of a Kṣatriya is circular; that of a Vaiśya is without a rim.
"I bring forth these waters, free from disease, which drive away disease."

"By means of *ṛta* (truth), I bring forth the waters together with *amṛta* (immortality) and life-force. Having accepted [the alms] with these words, he should practice the wandering for alms (*bhikṣācaryā*). A Brāhmaṇa should say, "Lady, give alms"; a Kṣatriya, "Lady, give the middle [portion]"; a Vaiśya, "Lady, give the last [portion].
He should approach four, six, or eight women who are not widows and who do not refuse.
Some say that one should first [inform] one's mother;
having informed the teacher,
one should remain silent and sit for the twilight devotions before leaving the village.

Standing facing the east, having recited the Sāvitrī three times: "O Lord of the paths, may I reach the end of this path with well-being. That wisdom which is among the Apsarases and that mind which is among the Gandharvas..."
"May that divine and human intelligence enter into me here"—
having returned with these words, he should tend the fire.
He should sweep around [the fire] with the verse, "This hymn for you who are worthy.
He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula, "You are fuel; may we prosper. He places a second one with the formula, "You are a kindler; may we be kindled."
"I have today entered the waters," with these words he worships [the fire].
"Unite me with luster," with these words he should wipe his face.
"O Agni, whatever ascetic heat we enter through ascetic heat and through the practice of celibacy..."
O venerable ones, you who are dear to sacred learning, possessed of great longevity and excellent intelligence:
I have brought fuel for Agni, the vast Jātavedas;
may that Jātavedas bestow upon me faith and wisdom.

"svāhā! With these words he places a fuel-stick on the fire. "Anoint me with brilliance! Anoint me with luster! Anoint me with the splendor of sacred knowledge! With these words he should wipe his face.

With the formula, "O Agni, you are the upholder of life," he touches the limbs according to their respective forms. With the successive formulas beginning with "May there be stability here," having touched the shoulder and the neck while reciting "Arcis," he should touch the forehead with the words "Bestow radiance upon us. There is sprinkling of water around [the fire] at the beginning and at the end.
He gives a choice gift and an upper garment to the teacher and to the Brahman priest.
He should eat food that is not pungent or salty for twelve nights;
according to some, it should be free from pungent substances.
When the twelve nights or the six nights have passed, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north,

he should sacrifice a *sthālīpāka* offering to Savitṛ at the foot of a *palāśa* tree or another sacrificial tree with the *Sāvitra* formula; then, after performing the *jaya* offerings and so forth with clarified butter,
but before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, he should cast his girdle and staff into the water.
"In that very place he should eat the remains of the oblation"— so says the Śruti.
From the initiation ceremony onwards, he should observe the vows.
By the rules for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), the instructions for the observances (*vrata*) are explained.

Wearing clothes from a path, with his hair matted, subsisting on the practice of begging for alms, and carrying a staff made of splinters, he should wear a girdle of sevenfold *muñja* grass; he should not be contrary to his teacher and should perform all tasks for him.
Whatever [the teacher] might approach him with, that he should give to him.
He should not share a bed with one who is associated with many [women]; he should not mount a chariot with him. (VGrs 6.4–6.6)
One should not live with [such a person].
(6.7) One should not converse for the sake of a monastery. (6.8) One should not keep gold for the sake of personal pleasure. (6.9)
One should avoid all physical contact with women.
One should not bathe like a staff.
One should not enter the water.
One should not sleep during the day.
One should practice the celibate life of the three Vedas.
Restraining the senses, one should subsist on almsfood in the evening and in the morning.
He should tend the sacred fire in the evening and in the morning;

he should sleep on the ground, live under the authority of his teacher, and obtain food—provided it is not salted—without asking, solely through the teacher’s grace. He should eat while maintaining silence.
One should avoid honey and meat.
One should not look at a woman who is naked or whose clothing is disarrayed.
He should carry a staff made from the wood of a *yūpa* tree.
He should not strike a cow with this [staff], nor a Brāhmaṇa.
He should not go to dancing or singing,
nor should he perform these himself.
He shall not shave [his hair].
(VGrs 6.25) He may have his top-knot matted, or he may have all his hair matted. (VGrs 6.26) His garment shall be made of hemp, linen, or animal skin. (VGrs 6.27)
A red garment or blanket made of deer-skin is for a Brāhmaṇa, one of Ruru-deer skin for a Kṣatriya, and one of goat-skin for a Vaiśya.
According to this rule, he should practice studentship (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years regarding a single Veda;
twenty-four years for two Vedas; thirty-six years for three Vedas; and forty-eight years for all of them.
"Or until he has mastered it;
one who is afflicted by impurity, weak, and emaciated, having bathed, obtains everything that is desired by his mind.
"In this manner, one studies well according to the Dharma."
Having studied the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, as well as the Kalpa and Mīmāṃsā, one is a Yājñika; having studied the Vaktra, Pada, and Smṛti, one is an Aicchika.
These two are Snātakas.
Any other who has studied the Veda is a Śrotriya.
For him, bathing is not required. Having sat down and placed his arms between his knees, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times.
He should wipe [his hands] twice and touch the apertures of the head.
Now, the initiation for the Caturhotṛ formulas lasts for one year.
Having poured the two libations (āghāra) and offered the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), he should offer the Caturhotṛ formula according to its own ritual procedure;
together with the Pañcahotṛ and the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ, he should finally offer the Saptahotṛ.
Having offered the oblations and given the vow-food, he should cause [the student] to recite the first two *anuvākas*.
Then follows the initiation for the *agni-vrata* and the *aśvamedha*, lasting either one year or twelve nights.
Having offered the six oblations with the hymn beginning "Ākūtam agnim" and having given the vow-food, he should cause him to recite the first eight *anuvākas*.
He should fetch water three times a day, three jars each time;
and he should collect three bundles of fuel. He should sleep on ashes, on cow-dung, on sand, or on the bare ground.
He should not enter the water.

When the year is completed, having sacrificed to Agni with an offering of cake mixed with ghee, he should cause [the student] to recite the Vātsapra hymn. According to the Smṛti rules, as long as the study continues, he should perform the specific rites for each section (*kāṇḍavrata*) and offer oblations at the beginning and end for the sake of the fire-sacrifice.
Then he should entrust him [to the guardians]: "I entrust you to Agni; I entrust you to Vāyu;
I entrust you to Sūrya."
"I entrust you to Prajāpati.
By this, the Aśvamedha is explained.
Having offered oblations with the ninth Anuvāka, one should worship with the tenth.
One should approach the horse with fodder, a place for water, and water itself.
With these two mantras, one should undertake the vow of the Traividya.
The Pravargya rite is to be studied in secret.
In its secret section are the undertaking of the vow, the fuel-sticks, and the mantra.
(VGrs 7.18) He should stand during the day and remain seated during the night, restrained in speech. (VGrs 7.19) On the parvan days, he should likewise observe this practice. (VGrs 7.20)
And he should have his hair matted (*jaṭila*).
(VGrs 7.21) The *pravargya* rite does not take place for less than a year.
(VGrs 7.22) Vārāha Gṛhya-sūtra, 8.1–2.
During the rainy season, he performs the opening ceremony for the Vedic lessons under the asterism Śravaṇa,
or under Hasta;
some say on the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada.
Then he offers the oblation:
"Thou art named Apvā; may I attain thy delighter. For I have indeed received from my father the wisdom of immortality."
I have been born like the sun. Svāhā! Your name is Apvā; may I attain your pleasure.
Through my father’s power, I have grasped the wisdom of immortality;
I have been born like the sun.
Svāhā!
Thus:
"You are named Yukti; you are named Yoga."
You are named Mati; you are named Sumati; you are named Sarasvatī.
"You are named Sarasvān.
To this one should append: "Of that [name] of yours, of that [name] of yours. "To the yoke, svāhā!"
Svāhā to the impulse! Svāhā to the joining!
Svāhā to the exertion!

Saying "Svāhā to the one striving," and with the *jaya* and other formulas, he offers oblations of clarified butter before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering if he desires the application of yoga for his pupils;
then he mutters: "I shall speak the Ṛta, I shall speak the Truth, I shall speak the Brahman; may that protect me, may it protect the speaker; may it protect me, may it protect the speaker."
May my speech be established in my mind; may my mind be established in my speech. Bestow long life upon me openly!
You are the voices of the Veda.
May the meters attend us; we commence the recitations of the study periods.
With *darbha* grass in hand, having recited the Sāvitrī three times— beginning with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"— as well as the first three Anuvākas and likewise one from each of the Aṅgas,
and [the verse] "Who yokes you? (RV 10.13.1),
these are his non-study periods.

According to the Śruti, there is no rain during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa when lightning flashes or thunder rolls; however, it may rain at any time if there is lightning, thunder, or meteors, or if sounds exceeding two syllables are heard. Others say this applies according to local custom.
Having studied for four and a half months, or five and a half months, or having studied the *Dīkṣaṇāyana* section, they then discontinue their studies according to this rule:
"I have spoken the Ṛta, I have spoken the Satya, I have spoken the Brahman; may that protect me and the speaker."
It has reached me; it has reached the speaker.
My speech is established in my mind; my mind is established in my speech. Bestow life upon me openly.
You are the voices of the Veda.
"May the meters breathe again; we release the lessons.
Having recited the end [of the Veda] with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" and "Who releases you?", one should not study for two nights (a *pakṣiṇī* night).
Or one with wings on both sides. Not beyond this [number] during the cloudy seasons. Lightning, thunder, and rain are considered "immediate" (ākālika) until the rain has ceased.
Now, those who are worthy of the Upaniṣads:
a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), one of good conduct, one who is wise, one who performs his duties, one who bestows wealth, one who is dear, or one who seeks knowledge through knowledge.
These are the sacred seats (*tīrthas*) of Brahman.
In the Vārāha Gṛhyasūtra, 9:
The Godāna ceremony is for a sixteen-year-old,
or for one who is about to study the sacred fires.
Agnigodāna is a descendant of Maitrāyaṇi.
(VGrs 9.1) The ritual procedure for the mantras regarding the formation of the matted locks has been stated.
(VGrs 9.2) There is an additional application of mantras for the generative organ and the armpits.
"When you, O barber, shave the hair and beard with a well-fashioned, sharp razor, cleanse the head and face; do not deprive him of his life. (VGrs 9.3)
One should bury the hair in the ground.
At the conclusion [of the study], one should give a cow as a gift.
Having been permitted by the teacher, one should bathe according to the Veda.
Having understood the meanings of the Vedic hymns (*chandas*), one who intends to bathe should cause a cow to be given;
he should honor his teacher.
Having bathed with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ," he should put on two unwashed garments.
"Thou art wealth; make me wealthy. For the sake of your splendor, for brilliance, and for Vedic luster, I entrust you [to this garment].
Thus he says. "Thou art the shade of all people," with these words he holds up the parasol.
He fastens on a garland: "The great lotus-wreath which the Aśvins wore..."
"I place this garland upon her, approved by all the gods.
Thus [he says].
With the words, "Thou art splendor," he should wear gold.
"O two deities, you are the supports; do not cause me distress," [with these words] he should take up his sandals.
"You are the support," [with these words] he should hold a bamboo staff and a water-pot containing water.
The teachers have declared these to be the perpetual vows.
From this point forward, one should wear two garments; "one must maintain beautiful clothing," so says the Śruti.

Having taken leave of his teachers and those dependent on his teachers, he should go to his own home. It is forbidden to exit by a side door, to converse with a woman in her menses, to share a bed with a woman in her menses, to speak ill of one's teacher, to lie down in an improper place, to stand in an improper place, to smile, to travel [inappropriately], to sing, or to recall [sensual pleasures].
One should avoid those [other means of livelihood].
Livelihood through officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) consists of:
gleaning ears of grain (*uñcha*), picking up single grains (*śila*), receiving gifts unasked, or requesting from virtuous people.
Or, if [the former] cannot be accomplished, the occupation of a Vaiśya;
he should abandon those pursuits that are incompatible with his private Vedic study.
(Vārāha Gṛhyasūtra 10.20–21)

Having subdued his anger, he should joyfully marry a wife who is joyful, not previously wedded to another, and younger than himself. Marriage is with those whose *pravara* lineages are not identical; [he may marry] beyond the seventh degree among paternal kinsmen, and beyond the fifth degree among maternal kinsmen and those related through the seed (*bījina*).
One should choose [a bride] under the asterisms of Kṛttikā, Svāti, and the Pūrvas;
one should marry under Mṛgaśiras, Śraviṣṭhā, and the Uttarās.
There are five factors that bring about marriage: wealth, beauty, learning, wisdom, and kinship.
If one gains nothing on the first occasion, he should give away his wealth; if on the second, his beauty;
if on the third, his learning.
But regarding wisdom and kinsmen, they dispute:
"May the paths be straight and free from thorns, by which our friends may go to choose what is desirable.
May Aryaman and Bhaga lead us together; O Gods, may the lordship of the household be well-governed."
Thus he addresses the bridegrooms as they depart.
He should marry a maiden who has relatives, who has not experienced sexual intercourse, and who is excellent, being one for whom no fire has been kindled.
He should perform a test of her discernment.
One should bring four clods of earth: a clod from a furrow, a clod from an altar, a clod of cow dung, and a clod from a cemetery.
He should say, "Choose one of these.
If he should choose the clod from a cemetery, he must not marry her.
One should marry an unwed woman according to the *brāhma* or *śaulka* rites.
One should give a chariot drawn by a hundred [oxen], or a pair of cattle.
One should seat both the groomsmen and the bridegroom’s kinsmen upon thorny branches.
The former [balls] should be for those who have children; the latter, for those whose daughters are young.
Having made four balls of cow dung, he should give two to one group and likewise two to the other group.
They should say, "No wealth."
"Neither sons nor cattle," say the kinsmen.
"I give;
I accept," he says three times regarding the gift for a Brahmin.
They should shrink away from the shoulder that has been prepared.
(VGrs 10.17) The Magadhan should call out "Ānanda" three times.
(VGrs 10.18) Vārāha Gṛhyasūtra, 11.18–19.
Six are worthy of the *arghya* offering: the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), one for whom one performs a marriage, a king, a *snātaka*, and a friend.
(VGrs 11.1) They do not offer the *arghya* to those who are not related by marriage until a full year has passed, except in the case of a sacrificial ritual or a wedding. (VGrs 11.2)
One whose father is still living should not accept the *arghya* offering.
Then they honor him:

having poured honey into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup (*camasa*) filled with curd, and having covered it with a larger vessel, [he recites]: "Thou art the milking of Virāj; thou art the milking of Virāj."
"May I obtain the milking of Virāj; may the milking of the Padyā-Virāj be in me"—with these words he awaits the honey-mixture being brought forward.
Having accepted the two *viṣṭara* grass mats with a verse addressed to Savitṛ, he spreads them upon the seat with their tips pointing north, saying: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom.
"I am the summit of those who are like me, like the rising sun."
"I make that person low who would attack me," saying this,
he sits down upon one [of them].
"May you not trample me today," saying this, he pulls the other one beneath his feet.
To him who is seated on a grass mat, he recites each verse three times.
He replies, "Not so,
sir," and "May we not come to harm."
The water for sipping is presented first.
He sips water with the formula, "Thou art the underlayer of immortality.
He washes his feet with the *padya* water.
He touches the *argha* offering.
Then he brings it forward.
Having accepted the *madhuparka* and the two mats on both sides with the *Sāvitra* formula, he places it on the ground with the words: "I set thee on the back of Aditi."

Having established [the vessel] and having set it down, he looks at it with the formula, "With the eye of Suparṇa Garutman, I look upon thee. Having pointed out the directions one by one with his span, saying, "Homage to Rudra, the sitter in the vessel," he mixes [the contents] with three fingers—the thumb and the ring finger—while reciting the three verses beginning, "The winds, honey for the righteous one. (VGrs 11.16)
"May truth, fame, and fortune attend me"—with these words, he eats the largest portion three times.
He gives what remains to a friend.
"Thou art the lid of immortality," with these words, he sips water.
With a sword in his hand, he addresses the cow:
"My evil has been struck down; may my evil be struck down!
You whom the Vasu gods lived alongside, the sister of the Ādityas, the mother of Rudra."
"Let them take hold of Aditi, the divine cow of men, for the honoring of the worthy ones.
Having thus issued the command, "Om,
do so," he should feed at least four Brahmins of different lineages (gotra), one by one, with either portions of the animal's limbs or milk-rice (pāyasa).
If she should release [the calf]: "She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality.
Let me speak forth to the discerning person: do not slay the cow, the sinless Aditi.
(VGrs 11.23) "Om! Release her; let her eat grass and drink water. (VGrs 11.24)
When this has been said, they immolate the animal.
Having washed their hands with "May Mitra be auspicious to us," they proceed according to their purpose.
Now, the ornamentation: "You are an ornament; may I be sufficient for everything.

I satisfy my out-breath and in-breath; I satisfy my common breath and diffused breath; I satisfy the form of my upward breath; I satisfy my sight and hearing. May I be one with good vision through my eyes, with good luster through my mouth, and with good hearing through my ears.
Regarding perfumes and garments:
"I shall put on [this garment]; I shall bestow glory; for the sake of long life, may I reach old age.
May you live a hundred abundant autumns, and may you, O venerable one, distribute riches and live on."

Having put on an unwashed garment, kindled the fire, and offered rice and barley with the *vyāhṛti* formulas, he should pronounce auspicious blessings. Now, at the wedding ceremony, [he approaches] the maiden who has fasted, bathed, and had her head washed, and is clothed in an unwashed garment with its fringe intact.

Having duly prepared the musical instruments arranged before the spread [sacrificial grass], he offers oblations before the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice to Vāc, Pathyā Svasti, Pūṣan, Pṛthivī, Agni, Senā, Dhenā, Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, Paṅkti,
Virāj, Rākā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Tvaṣṭṛ, Āśā, Sampatti, Bhūti, and Nirṛti.
He should offer oblations to Anumati, Parjanya, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Having smeared his hands with the remainder of the clarified butter, he wipes the girl's face, saying: "I make her dear to her husband, to the brothers-in-law, and to the father-in-law.
May Agni unite you for the sake of favor; be one who finds favor with your husband."
"May the goddess Ilā, whose foot is dripping with ghee, unite you with good fortune— Indrāṇī, Agnāyī, Aśvinī,
Rāṭ, Vāk, Ilā, Dyauḥ, and Arundhatī. Thus it is said.

He consecrates all the musical instruments with the mantra: "That which sounds forth in four ways—in the fire, in the wind, and that which is great; that which they have placed among cattle and among Brahmins—may that auspicious one sound forth here. (VGrs 13.3)
Having adorned all the musical instruments, the maiden plays them: "Speak auspiciously, O drum; speak well for the sake of good offspring, O you with the face of a bull!
Let the maidens play, being well-disposed, together with Indrāṇī, of equal age and of one nest.
Prajāpati, who dwells among living beings—may they extend their progeny, being well-disposed."
"May he delight these creatures for the sake of procreation, and may he himself delight us, bestowing peace.
Thus they utter the *kārālikā* verses.
One should sprinkle the girl with water [reciting]:
"In the hole of the chariot, in the hole of the cart, in the hole of the yoke of Śatakratu..."
"Indra made the wife of the childless woman threefold, possessing the luster of the sun.
Having said this, he then gives her an unwashed garment.
Then he binds her with a cord of *darbha* grass: "I bind you together with the milk of the earth; I bind you together with the waters and the plants."
"I bind you together with offspring and wealth; being thus bound, press out the portion for the gods.
Then, having caused her to grasp the hem of her garment, he leads her forward, saying: "Be one whose eye is not terrible, one who does not strike her husband."
"Come, O auspicious one, well-disposed toward our livestock, full of splendor;
as a wife with long life and progeny, finding the light of heaven, led by Indra, come to dwell among us.
(VGrs 14.3)
Sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and inspecting—these are the preparations for the ground at the time of the fire-ritual, to be performed everywhere according to the specific requirements.
(VGrs 14.4) To the west of the fire, on a mat, on a reed-mat, or on *darbha* grass, is the seat.

(VGrs 14.5) On a clean spot of ground, [one should prepare the site] with *śamī*, *śamaka*, and *śyāmāka* grains; with *priyaṅgu*, *dūrvā*, and white mustard seeds as available; and with fragrant substances, milk, and fruits from trees, as well as green leaves, *kuśa* grass, barley, and so forth.

Having consecrated the water with gold by reciting the *anuvāka* beginning with "cānnair yā oṣadhayaḥ" and "samanyā yanti," as well as the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ," he should bring forward the water-pitcher containing the consecrated water (*praṇītā*).
While the oblations of parched grain (*lāja*) are being offered, his brother or a student (*brahmacārī*) should hold it up and maintain it to the south.
The mother, or another woman who is not a widow, [places] the prepared parched grains mixed with *śamī* leaves in a winnowing basket to the south.

Having prepared the clarified butter, having addressed the *brahman*, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, and having poured the two libations (*āghāra*) and offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*),
he then makes the oblations.
Svāhā to Agni, the knower of people!
Svāhā to Soma, the knower of people! Svāhā to Gandharva, the knower of people!
Soma first obtained you; Gandharva obtained you next;
Agni was your third husband; I, born of man, am your fourth—svāhā!
"Soma gave [her] to the Gandharva; the Gandharva gave [her] to Agni.
And Agni gave me wealth and sons, as well as this woman.
Thus.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," verse by verse.
Regarding the *jayas*, the Śruti states: "In whatever rite one desires success, there one should offer the *jayas*";
they are to be offered as previously described.
To intention, thee, svāhā! To prosperity, thee, svāhā! To desire, thee, svāhā!
Hail to you for protection!
Hail to you for prosperity! Hail to you for success!
With a Ṛg-verse, [I offer] the Stoma to Prajāpati; Bhūḥ Svāhā!
And [he recites] "And you, O Agni, are... (AYĀŚ CĀGNE 'SĪTI).
To the north of the fire, having stationed the girl facing east upon *darbha* grass, the groom, standing in front of her facing west, takes her hand with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take your hand, O [Name]. (DEVASYA TE SAVITUḤ PRASAVE 'ŚVINOR BĀHUBHYĀM PŪṢṆO HASTĀBHYĀM HASTAṂ GṚHṆĀMY AMUṢYĀI).
Then, as at the initiation ceremony, he takes her hand with his own non-empty hand:

"I take your hand for the sake of good fortune, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Purandhi—the gods have given you to me for the state of being a householder."
Speech arose upward before the gods and the asuras— O Sarasvatī, you whom I have extended at the forefront of all that exists; O auspicious one, rich in vigor, favor this [sacrifice]!
We shall today sing that verse by which all that has come to be and this entire world came into existence—that verse which is the highest mind of women:
"You are she; I am he. I am he;
you are she. I am heaven; you are earth. I am the Bṛhat; you are the Rathantara."
I am the seed; you are the bearer of the seed.
I am the Sāman; you are the Ṛc. I am the mind; you are speech. Be devoted to me; be born after me.
"Let us two both create progeny for the sake of producing a male son;
O Sūnṛtā, [create] for the sake of prosperity, a son, and offspring here.
Thus. (VGrs 14.13)
He should lead her around the fire, keeping it to his right.
To the west of the fire, upon darbha grass, he places a stone, saying: "Tread upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm.
May all the gods grant you a hundred autumns of life."
Thus [he says].
At this very point, he gives her a second garment.
Over the fire, into her joined palms, the brother or a *brahmacārin* shall pour the parched grains (*lāja*), having first spread a base layer [of ghee] underneath.
One should offer those [grains] after they have been sprinkled with clarified butter, without interruption.
The performer should recite the mantra:
"This noble woman, scattering parched grains, speaks thus."
May my husband be long-lived; may my kinsmen prosper.
The maidens have now worshipped the god Aryaman and Agni;
may that god Aryaman release us from here and release me from there.
"svāhā! Thus [he says].
"May I be a mother of heroes and have a living husband," he should cause her to recite at every stage.
"In the beginning, I led Sūryā around for you together with her bridal procession;
O Agni, give the wife back to her husbands along with offspring"— with these words, he should lead her around a second time.
In the same way, the third [offering] is identical from the point of placement onwards; [the verse is]:
"Pūṣan, the god..."
The two oblations are with the verses beginning "Varuṇaṃ nu devam.
The rite from "kanyāgnim ayakṣata" is the same [as before].
Having completed the fourth [oblation] with the word "kāmena," he should pour clarified butter over it twice and offer it in the eastern part of the northern half of the fire.
Then he makes her take seven steps toward the east: "One for food—may Viṣṇu lead you; two for strength;
three for the increase of wealth."
Four for the sake of prosperity,
five for offspring,
six for the seasons.

"For each of the seven officiating priests (hotṛs), he should append the formula 'May Viṣṇu lead you' starting from the second [step]. At the seventh step, while she is looking at him, he gazes at her, saying: 'Be my companion for seven steps; may I attain friendship with you; through friendship with you, may I not suffer harm.'"
"May he release you from the noose of Varuṇa, with which Savitṛ, the very gracious one, bound you.
In the womb of Dhātṛ, in the world of the well-performed deed, may I be joyful together with my husband.
Having thus untied the cord, they purify themselves with a water-pot while reciting the section beginning, "May the Fathers purify me."
Some say [he should recite] the *āpohiṣṭhīya* verses.
"This bride is auspicious; having come together, look upon her.
Bestowing good fortune upon her, depart as you please."
Thus [it is said].
The remainder is explained by the rules for the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking). Regarding the separation [of the fires]: [the procedure is as follows].
The oblations beginning with "yena dyaur ugrā" should be performed at the wedding;
however, there are no parched grains (*lājā*) when the hand is not taken [in marriage].
The stepping forward and the purification (*mārjana*) are the same [as in other rites].
The two auspicious marks on both sides of the chariot, the dark winds that fly toward the front,
the far-reaching arrow, and the winged ones full of vigor— may these fires, being full, carry us across to safety.
Thus he consecrates the wheel:

"O Sūryā, mount this chariot which is well-adorned with *kiṃśuka* flowers, made of *śalmali* wood, multiform, golden-hued, with a good pole and beautiful wheels; ascend the path of immortality and go to your home by that way in safety."
Thus he should superimpose:

"May the deities approach me; may the sacred formulation (*brahman*) and great heroism approach me; may the dominion (*kṣatra*) and whatever strength there is approach me; may whatever strength there is come to me."
Thus he mutters as he is about to depart:
"May the deities follow me; may the sacred word and great heroism follow me; may the ruling power and whatever glory there is follow me; may whatever glory there is come to me."
Having thus caused [the guest] to proceed eastward and having turned clockwise, he should pay homage at a tree possessing its proper characteristics or at a *caitya*.
At a solitary tree, he mutters: "Homage to Rudra who dwells in the solitary tree," and also:
"Those who are tawny among the trees."
At a crossroads, [one should offer] with the mantra: "Homage to Rudra, who dwells at the crossroads," and also with:
"Those who guard the paths of the ways.
At a cremation ground, [one should offer] with: "Homage to Rudra, who dwells in the cremation ground."
And [he recites]: "Those who are the lords of beings," and while drinking,
"Homage to Rudra, who dwells in the vessel," and "Those who pierce into foods."
Those who [call] "the holy fords" at the ford—
where the waters were to be crossed— [let them offer] to the one who has surpassed the ocean, to the one who knows the ways, to the lord of the rivers;
let them sacrifice to Viśvakarman, the drinker of all rivers.
"May the oblation be invincible on every side"—with these words, he should offer handfuls of water into the waters.

He should offer as many handfuls of water as there are friends for whom he desires well-being. "I offer nectar into the mouth; I bestow life upon the breath. Together with the Brahman, may we cross over death."

With the mantra *prāsahā* he performs an offering; with the mantra *aditir eva mṛtyuṃdheyam*, he should sip water three times and wipe his mouth twice. If the axle-pin or the yoke-pin should break, he should kindle a fire right there, perform an offering of a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni, and offer portions of clarified butter with the *jaya* formulas and so forth, ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
At the time of twilight on the following day, he should cause [the bride] to enter the house.
From the chariot or the domestic fire, he spreads a continuous line of *ulapa* grass.
By means of that, he approaches her.
"I enter the houses with a cheerful mind, not slaying heroes, but full of heroes and very gracious;
carrying nourishment and sprinkling clarified butter, may I enter them with a cheerful mind.
With these words, he enters the dwelling which contains the kindled fire, water, and herbs.
Under the asterism Revatī, Rohiṇī, or as prescribed for an auspicious occasion,
having sat upon the hide of a bull,
he should then cause a student who has both his father and mother living to sit upon her lap.

He should fill his cupped hands with fruit, or with sesame seeds and rice. Having shown her the Dhruva star while reciting, "O imperishable one, firm one, wife of the firm one! May we see the firm [star] forever," and having shown her the Seven Sages and Arundhatī, he should sacrifice a *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to Prajāpati, followed by the *jaya* and other oblations of clarified butter.
Before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having poured curd into the remainder of the clarified butter, he eats of the curd three times, saying: "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan.
Then [he says]: "Like the wheel of a draft-ox, let your mind follow after me alone."
"You see me and you see the sun; do not set your mind on others.
This dwelling together like that of the ruddy goose—this is the bond we have established.
With these words, he hands the remainder to his wife.
She eats it silently.
For one year, they both joyfully observe the vow of celibacy;
or for twelve nights, three nights, or one night.

In the same manner, having performed the fourth [offering], he offers eight oblations of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) with the verse "Hiraṇyagarbha" (RV 10.121.1), and oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *jaya* formulas and others, prior to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Then, while the knot of her garment is being tied, he consecrates it on her left shoulder with the formula: "May Pūṣan tie the knot for you.
Four women who are not widows perform this.
He gives gold to them.
He should not go abroad for a year,
nor for twelve nights, nor for three nights, nor for one night.
Vārāhagṛhyasūtra 16:
They two bring them together [with the verses]:
"I beheld thee with my mind, O thou who art observant, born of fervor, overcome by fervor."
Bestowing offspring here and wealth here, be propagated with progeny, O you who desire a son!
I beheld you with my mind as you were meditating, yearning for your own body at the proper season. May the young woman rise up toward me; be propagated with progeny, O you who desire a son!

O Prajāpati, take pleasure in my body; may I be Tvaṣṭṛ through my heroic sons, and Indra through my power. May we, together with Indra and the gods, clothe ourselves in plants; may we become the parents of many men. I have generated offspring upon the earth; I have placed the germ within the plants.
"I am within all worlds; I bear sons for my offspring"—thus they mutter, alternating with the woman and others.
"May he grant [offspring]," he says while touching her buttocks.
"Janat" refers to the people above;
"bṛhat" refers to that which has been born and established.
Then, in her third month of pregnancy, on a day when the moon is not visible under a male asterism, or having fasted on that day, he should bathe and [put on] unwashed [clothes].

Having covered her with a garment and having ground the shoots of a *nyagrodha* sprout with water, he should pour it into her right nostril while reciting these two verses: "Hiraṇyagarbha" and "Adbhyaḥ saṃbhṛtaḥ.
Then he should touch her right side, saying: "Male is Agni, male is Indra, male is the god Bṛhaspati."
A male is Agni and Vāyu; a male is the embryo within your womb.
Mitrā-Varuṇa are two males, and both Aśvins are males.
Give birth to a male embryo; let a male be born after you.
With these two [verses].

Then, in her fifth, sixth, or seventh month of pregnancy, having bathed her with auspicious substances, and having performed an offering of a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Prajāpati, and having offered oblations of clarified butter with the *jaya* and subsequent formulas, before the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, she causes all her hair to be loosened while she is seated on *darbha* grass behind the fire, [with the verse]: "O god, you who possess self-power (*svadhāvan*), you become Aryaman when you bear the secret [beauty] of maidens."
“They anoint the sage as if with well-made [butter], when you make the two spouses well-disposed.
Having thus smeared both hands with fresh butter, she combs all the hair together.
“Indrāṇī made a comb; let it glide through her parting,” saying this, she takes up the comb.
Furthermore, he should perform the dressing of his wife's hair with the formula "Agni [is] the husband.
With a porcupine quill and a branch of the *śamī* tree together with its leaves,
he should [place it] upon her while she is pregnant, [praying for] a male child who shall live long and reach a hundred years.
"May he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns.
With these words, he parts her hair with a three-white [grass].
Then her husband binds her hair in two parts with a blue-and-red thread or with wool from a living animal.
Vārāhagṛhyasūtra, 17:
Now we shall explain the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

(1) Therein, for those [offerings] beginning with the evening and morning [oblations], having swept around, strewn [grass] around, and sprinkled water around as in the Agnihotra, it should be performed in the evening and in the morning; so say some. (2)
Or, from the prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering.
One should offer oblations to Agni, Soma, Prajāpati, Dhanvantari, Vāstoṣpati, the Viśvedevas, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
One should then present the bali-offering with what remains.
[He offers] mixed with curds and honey: to Agni in the east, to Yama in the south, to Soma in the west, to Varuṇa in the north; in the center, to Varuṇa and Aryaman, and to Brahmāṇaspati.
[He offers] to Agni, to the Earth, to Vāyu, to the Atmosphere, to Sūrya, to the Sky, to the Moon, and to the Nakṣatras.
To the Waters at the place of the water-jar.
"To the plants and trees" in the middle of the room; "To Kāma,
to the householder" at the place of the bed.
And for Śrī;
for the Rākṣasas within the shelter;
for Ākāśa with the two stalks of the *sthalikā* plant.
Having departed silently, [he should offer] the *kavya* in the upper shelter. To the east, he should append the formula: "To the ancestors, *svadhā*! (VGrs 17.14–15).
And at the end of "namas," [he says]:
"Those Brahmins who are in the eastern direction;
those gods and those beings whom I approach—may they grant me well-being."
In the south;
in the west;
in the north.

In the verse beginning with "ūrdhvāyām," one should attach the phrase "ye brāhmaṇāḥ" everywhere. Having fed learned Brāhmaṇas food that is unctuous and free of meat, one should have them recite for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
At the conclusion of the *bali* offering, whatever blessing he may desire, that he should pronounce.
The householder says: "Oṃ, may the food be inexhaustible.
Having given alms, he should eat his evening meal at dawn.
Having returned from a journey abroad, he should stand at the entrance of his home.
